catalog_quote: An intonation group is a sequence of two or more syllables with highest intonation on one syllable. The close of the syllable following an intonation peak ends the intonation group. (* indicates an intonation peak.) qE-genát ka 'Are you going?' qE-génat kÉ-qen 'Are you going now?' Clause length utterances have at least one intonation peak and certain of these may have two at the discretion of the speaker. qE-genat kE-qen dáqan 'You will go also.' ... a, when it occurs in an ultima, is replaced by E before the intonation peak. qE-dúma 'He will go along.' qE-dumá qa 'I'll go along.' qE-dumE kÉy-qen 'We'll go along.' qE-dumE qÉ-dea 'I'll just go along.' qEbága 'waterfall' qEbagá ded 'Just a waterfall.' qEbagE qémbes 'So it's a waterfall is it?' 2.3.3 In the vowel position before ultima-final glottal stop, a occurs only when the intonation peak falls on the preceding syllable or when it (a) is immediately followed by another a. Otherwise it is replaced by E. bátaq 'child' batÉq pa 'Still a child.' batáq a 'I am a child.' díyaq 'There.' diyÉq ded 'Just there.' diyÉq ka 'Go there.' ... [p. 6:] bégas 'rice' dúqen 'There is.' nEkEgénat qen 'He left already.' ... sikámi, geli, mErégen is kEnámi he qEgkEqulaqúla 'As for us, friend, our life is very hard.' mEbegat qútEw se qúled 'The snake is very heavy' [Elkins prints the peak as * above the vowel; rendered here as an acute. q = glottal stop; E = e reflecting *a]

sweep_summary: Western Bukidnon Manobo is not in the catalog. The single keyword hit (Elkins 1983 'Culture stress and conversion', Notes on Scripture in Use 5) is a false positive: acculturative stress in a missiological study, not word stress. this search of works with stress in the title went beyond the keyword list via the OLAC listing for mbb (75 entries, downloaded through the Internet Archive) and SIL Language & Culture Archives records, and downloaded the previously unobtained Elkins 1963 'Morphophonemics Western Bukidnon Manobo' typescript, the 1970 SIL PL 26 published grammar, Pittman 1968 (SIL-UND WP 12, exercise 16 on WBM), Buenconsejo 2006 (uwaging prosody), the 1966 WBM wordlist sheets, the Manobo alphabet primer and Elkins 1980 (verbs). Result: every first-hand Elkins source describes prominence only as an 'intonation peak' on the penult of the intonation group, shifting to the host-final syllable before a monosyllabic clitic and conditioning a > e in the pre-peak ultima (1962/63 sect. 2.3; 1963 ms sect. 2.21; 1967 diss. fn. 4); the 1953 phonemes paper explicitly excludes stress, and the 1970 grammar's phonology section is an inventory only. No source states a lexical stress rule or a stress contrast. Still unread: the introduction (sects. 1-3) of Elkins 1968 Manobo-English Dictionary (JSTOR i20019115; high priority — the likeliest explicit stress statement) and its reviews by Wolff 1969 (Language 45:686-687, DOI 10.2307/411455) and Reid 1971 (Foundations of Language 7:449-450, JSTOR 25000550). and logged in there.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Elkins describes prominence as a pitch ('intonation') peak whose position is fixed relative to the end of the intonation group: the peak is always followed by exactly one syllable, i.e. it falls on the penultimate syllable of the group. A word said alone carries the peak on its penult (bátaq, díyaq, qEbága, qE-dúma); a following monosyllabic enclitic is grouped with the word and pulls the peak onto the word's final syllable (batáq a, qEbagá ded, qE-dumá qa, diyÉq ka). The 1967 dissertation restates this as a 3-4-1 pitch contour with the highest pitch (4) on the penult and the lowest (1) on the ultima of the group. Antepenultimate (pre-peak) a is neutralised with e, i.e. pretonic reduction.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. Elkins notes only that clause-length utterances may carry two intonation peaks (two groups) at the speaker's discretion; Blust 2013:255 fn.35 infers that WBM full reduplications (alaŋʔalaŋ, basavasa) 'carry two primary stresses'.
new_statements.exceptions: No lexical exceptions or contrastive pairs are given; peak placement varies only through phrasing (e.g. 'qE-genat kÉy-qen guntáqan' with two peaks vs 'qE-genat kEy-en guntáqan' with one, answering different questions). Elkins 1953:108 had declined to describe stress at all for 'insufficient evidence'.
new_statements.domain_note: The statement is framed as intonation, not lexical stress: the domain is the 'intonation group' (content word plus following enclitic particles), so the reading 'fixed: penultimate syllable' holds for citation forms and for the group as a whole; a stricter reading of the same passage would be 'phrase-level prominence only' (penultimate phrasal prominence, no word-level stress claimed). No accessible Elkins source lists stress as a phoneme (1953, 1967 inventory, Reid 1971 p.32), consistent with non-contrastive, position-fixed prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Elkins 1962/1963 and 1967 describe Western Bukidnon Manobo proper (data from Barandias, Pangantocan, Bukidnon; west2555). Elkins 1953 'Southern Bukidnon Manobo' is a different variety (informant at Damulog, Kibawe, speaking a Dongoanen/Kulamanen mix with Ilianen influence), which Elkins 1967:4 fn.8 calls 'a slightly different dialect'; it should not be equated with west2555 without qualification (Kulamanen is usually placed with Ilianen Manobo, ilia1236).

new_statements.reading: Elkins never uses the word 'stress' for WBM. Prosodic prominence is described as an 'intonation peak' that falls on the penult of an intonation group (Elkins 1962/1963 sect. 2.3: the peak is followed by exactly one syllable; 1967 diss. fn. 4 p. 61: highest pitch on the penult, lowest on the ultima), so a word in isolation has its peak on its penult, and when a monosyllabic clitic follows, the peak moves to the word-final syllable (eduma -> eduma a; bata' -> bete' a), which conditions the a > e neutralisation in the pre-peak ultima. Read as a word-stress statement this is 'penultimate, phrase-level, no lexical contrast reported'; but it is explicitly framed as intonation, not word stress, and none of the first-hand sources (1953 phonemes paper excludes suprasegmentals; 1962/63; 1963 ms; 1967 diss; 1970 book; 1971 Reid list; 1966 wordlist) states a lexical stress rule or stress contrast. The 1968 dictionary introduction (unread, JSTOR) remains the one place an explicit stress statement might exist.

sources.note: Never uses the word 'stress'. Sect. 2.1 defines ultima/penult/antepenult and states a and e never contrast in antepenult syllables (a -> e when shifted to antepenult by suffixation). Sect. 2.3 (pp.4-5) defines the 'intonation group' so that the intonation peak (marked *) is always followed by exactly one syllable, i.e. the pitch peak sits on the penult of the group; isolated words are marked with the peak on the penult (bátaq 'child', díyaq 'there', qEbága 'waterfall', qE-dúma), and a following monosyllabic enclitic moves the peak to the host's last syllable (batáq a, qEbagá ded, qE-dumá qa).…

sources.note: Ethnomusicology of the sung epic: verse lines are syllabic meter (seven to nine syllables, one pulse each); 'It is not possible to scan the lines for a neat number of feet and groupings of syllables according to stresses.. the relevant meter used in uwaging is SYLLABIC METER, not syllable-stress meter' (p. 17); recited delivery has 'stresses ranging from two to three per line'. Nothing on word-level stress placement.
